Recover the transmission from the wreckage.

data.name: The Foxglove Trace
data.description:
A hobbyist had a quiet obsession: figuring out, without asking anyone, which unknown place they kept drifting back to on autopilot. Their idea was to mine two signals their phone already recorded — step-count spikes and the strength of nearby Wi-Fi access points — on the theory that a place that truly matters shows up as you *moving around* near the same access point, over and over.

They never finished it. All that's left is a handful of files pulled off the old project folder: some scratch notes, a tiny config, one exported scan, and the log of the single run that actually worked.

No server, no service, nothing to connect to. This is pure offline forensics. Reconstruct the person's scoring rule from what the files imply — the movement cutoff that separates "walking" from "sitting still", and how a per-access-point score is built from signal strength and the trust weights — then apply it to the full export and name the place they kept returning to. The loudest access point is a trap; so is the one that appears most often. Get the rule right and exactly one place rises to the top.

The derived place name is the key to the flag. Submit it as `hiCTF{PlaceName}`, with the name spelled as the access point appears in the files.

**Files:** [abandoned-tracker.zip](https://hicon26-files-b19d71.nbg1.your-objectstorage.com/abandoned-tracker/5fb6cb4590ef410d/abandoned-tracker.zip)

data.name: Warden’s Maze
data.description:
A tiny terminal arcade game, served over a single TCP connection. You are a
dot in a Pac-Man-style maze: collect pellets, dodge the patrolling warden, and
explore. Dead in the centre is a vault — walled off with its own distinct tile
and sealed on every side. The prize sits inside it.

There is no key, no switch, no hidden door. By the ordinary rules of movement
the vault simply cannot be entered, and the movement code holds up to any
amount of poking. The way in is not a game mechanic — it is a genuine mistake
in the engine itself, and finding it means reverse engineering the provided
game binary: understanding how the maze is stored, how the renderer decides
what you can see, and the one place where that visibility code reaches into the
map with a hand-rolled index. Get a single step of that arithmetic to land
where the author never expected, and a wall becomes a floor.

The game binary is in the download; the live service runs that exact binary.
The validation token is minted per instance and only appears on a genuine win.
